title: Bringing work back together
objectives: Merge a branch and read what the merge did
Tell a fast-forward from a merge commit, and read both in `git log --graph`

screens.prose:
On experiment you made two commits, c3 and c4, and the new signal works. main has not moved since you branched. You bring the work into main:

```sh
$ git switch main
$ git merge experiment
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

screens.question: Tap the commit main should point to after the merge, so that it contains your work.

hints.text: main contains every commit behind the one it points to. Which commit has c3 and c4 behind it?
experiment's work ends here.
If main points at c4, following arrows back reaches c4, c3, c2 and c1. That is everything.

feedback.correct: main moves to c4 and now contains c3 and c4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the commit that has all your work behind it.

byKey.stayed: If main stayed on c2, it would not contain c3 or c4. The merge has to move main.
byKey.c3: From c3 you reach c2 and c1, but not c4. main would miss your last commit.
byKey.main: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.experiment: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.HEAD: Tap a commit, not a label.

explain.text: main was directly behind experiment, so git just slid main forward to c4. No new commit was needed. git reports this as `Fast-forward`.

screens.prose: A new situation. While you worked on experiment (c4, c5), a date fix, c3, landed on main. Now both branches have new commits.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

state.caption: On main. The branches split after c2.

screens.question: Suppose git slid main forward to c5, as before. Tap every commit main would then contain.

hints.text: Start at c5 and follow the arrows back.
This is where main would point after sliding.
From c5 the arrows go to c4, c2 and c1. c3 is not on that path.

feedback.correct: From c5 you reach c4, c2 and c1, but not c3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows back from c5 only.

byKey.kept-fix: c3 is not behind c5. Follow the arrows from c5: they go to c4, c2 and c1. main would lose the fix.
byKey.c3: c3 is not behind c5. Follow the arrows from c5: they go to c4, c2 and c1. main would lose the fix.
byKey.c1: Keep following arrows back from c5, all the way to c1.
byKey.HEAD: Tap only commits.

explain.text: Sliding main to c5 would leave c3, the date fix, behind. Sliding only works when main is directly behind the branch. Here it is not, so git needs another way.

canvas.caption: If main slid to c5, c3 would drop out

screens.prose: Instead, git makes a new commit, m, with **two** parents: c3 and c5. This is a **merge commit**. Sliding forward, as on the first screen, is called a **fast-forward**.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

screens.question: Tap every commit main contains now.

hints.text: Start at main. How many arrows leave m?
m has two arrows. Follow both.
From m you reach c3 and c5. From those, c2, c4 and c1. Count m itself too.

feedback.correct: main now contains all six commits, both lines of work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow every arrow back from main, including both of m's.

byKey.one-parent: You followed only one of m's arrows. A merge commit has two parents, so follow both.
byKey.no-merge: m is a commit too, the newest one on main. Include it.
byKey.m: m is a commit too, the newest one on main. Include it.
byKey.c4: m's second arrow leads to c5, and from there to c4. Follow both of m's arrows.
byKey.c1: Keep following arrows back, all the way to c1.
byKey.HEAD: Tap only commits.

explain.text: m points to both c3 and c5, so main reaches everything: the fix and your signal. Only main moved, because HEAD was on main. experiment still points at c5.

screens.prose:
You are still on main, at m. A minute later you run the same merge again:

```sh
$ git merge experiment
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

state.caption: On main, after the first merge

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: Nothing changes: git says Already up to date
git makes a second merge commit
options.why: A merge commit joins work main lacks. main already reaches c5, so there is nothing to join.

options.text: main moves back to c5
options.why: A merge never moves a branch backwards. It only adds what is missing.

options.text: A conflict, because the work is already there
options.why: Merging what you already have is harmless. git checks and stops.

hints.text: Does main already contain c5?
Follow m's second arrow.
main reaches c5 through m. So experiment has nothing main lacks.

feedback.correct: main already contains everything on experiment.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what experiment has that main lacks.

explain.text: main already reaches c5 through m, so experiment adds nothing. git prints `Already up to date.` and changes nothing.

screens.prose:
experiment is merged, so you tidy up:

```sh
$ git branch -d experiment
Deleted branch experiment (was 9be1d07).
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

screens.question: What did git delete?

options.text: Only the label experiment
The label and commits c4 and c5
options.why: You treated the branch as its own copy of the work. It is a label; c4 and c5 stay, reached through m.

options.text: The label, c4, c5 and the merge commit m
options.why: Deleting a label never removes commits that main still reaches.

options.text: Nothing: git refuses to delete a branch with commits
options.why: `-d` refuses only when the branch has commits that are not merged yet. These are in main.

hints.text: What is a branch?
main reaches c4 and c5 through m.
A branch is a label. Removing it leaves every commit main can still reach.

feedback.correct: Only the label went. c4 and c5 are still in main's history.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A branch is a label pointing at a commit.

byKey.commits: You treated the branch as its own copy of the work. It is a label; c4 and c5 stay, reached through m.

explain.text: The label is gone, but c4 and c5 are still reached through m. `git branch -d` checks this first. It refuses with not fully merged when deleting would strand commits.

screens.prose: `git log --oneline --graph` draws the same picture in text, newest first. Each `*` is a commit. The bars on the left are the arrows, drawn as two lanes that meet at the merge.
screens.question: Tap the lines for the commits made on experiment.

hints.text: The merge commit's message names the branch it brought in. Which lane joins it from the side?
The `|\` line is where the second lane splits off from the merge.
Commits in the right-hand lane, `| *`, came from experiment. The left lane is main.

feedback.correct: 9be1d07 and 3c88a10 sit in the experiment lane.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the stars in the right-hand lane.

byKey.took-main: 7d02e5b sits in the left lane, main's own line. Its star comes before the bar.
byKey.r4c0: 7d02e5b sits in the left lane, main's own line. Its star comes before the bar.
byKey.took-merge: a41f2c9 is the merge commit. It was made on main, to join the two lanes.
byKey.r0c0: a41f2c9 is the merge commit. It was made on main, to join the two lanes.
byKey.r6c0: 51aa3e4 comes before the split, so it is on both branches.
byKey.r1c0: That line is a pair of arrows, not a commit. Commits have a star.
byKey.r5c0: That line is where the lanes join back, not a commit. Commits have a star.

explain.text: The right-hand lane holds 9be1d07 and 3c88a10, your experiment commits. The left lane is main: 7d02e5b, then the merge a41f2c9. Below the `|/`, 51aa3e4 is where the lanes split.

screens.prose:
Same split as before, but this time you are on experiment. You want your signal in main, so you type:

```sh
$ git merge main
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

enter.caption: The merge commit m is drawn in. The labels are shown as they were before.

screens.question: Tap the commit main points to afterwards.

hints.text: A merge moves which branch: the one you name, or the one you are on?
HEAD points at experiment.
`git merge main` brings main's work into experiment, the branch you are on. main itself does not move.

feedback.correct: main has not moved. The merge went into experiment.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A merge moves only the branch HEAD is on.

byKey.moved-main: You expected main to receive the work. `git merge main` brings main into the branch you are on, experiment. main stays on c3.
byKey.c5: experiment moved from c5 to the new merge commit, and main was never at c5.
byKey.main: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.experiment: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.HEAD: Tap a commit, not a label.

explain.text: `git merge main` brought main's fix into experiment, so experiment moved to m. main did not move and still lacks your signal. To fill main, stand on main and run `git merge experiment`.

canvas.caption: experiment moved to m; main stayed on c3

screens.prose:
The pattern you used:

```sh
$ git switch main            # stand on the branch that receives
$ git merge experiment       # bring experiment in
$ git log --oneline --graph  # check the picture
$ git branch -d experiment   # remove the label
```

If main is directly behind, git fast-forwards. Otherwise it makes a merge commit with two parents.
screens.question: When does `git merge` make a merge commit?

options.text: When both branches have new commits since they split
Every time you merge
options.why: When main is directly behind the branch, git just slides it forward. That is a fast-forward.

options.text: Only when the same lines were changed
options.why: A merge commit is about the shape of the history. Most merge commits have no conflict at all.

options.text: When you delete the branch afterwards
options.why: Deleting a label happens after the merge and changes no commits.

hints.text: Compare the first screen with the second.
On the first screen main had no new commits, so git slid it. On the second, both had moved on.

feedback.correct: Two lines of new work need a commit to join them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the fast-forward with the split.

explain.text: A fast-forward is possible only when main is behind the branch on one line. Once both have new commits, a merge commit with two parents joins them.

screens.prose: main has 4 commits; the last wrote `results-2026-09.md`. You branch momentum-12m there and commit 3 times. Meanwhile a colleague commits a holiday-calendar fix to main. You merge momentum-12m into main.
screens.question: How many commits does `git log --oneline` on main list afterwards?

hints.text: Is this a fast-forward, or will there be a merge commit?
Both branches moved on, so there is a merge commit. Add 4 original, 1 fix, 3 branch commits and the merge commit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the original commits, the fix, the branch commits and anything the merge adds.

byKey.no-merge-commit: You left out the merge commit. Both branches moved on, so git cannot fast-forward; it adds one commit.
byKey.squashed: A merge keeps every commit from the branch. All 3 momentum commits appear, plus the merge commit.
byKey.branch-only: You left out the colleague's fix or the merge commit. Both are on main afterwards.

explain.text: main keeps its 4 commits and the fix, gains your 3 commits, and adds 1 merge commit: 9 in all. The commit that wrote the results note is still in that history. You can always check out that exact version again.

ideas: To merge, stand on the branch that receives and name the one to bring in. Only the branch HEAD is on moves.
If main is directly behind the branch, git fast-forwards. If both have new commits, it makes a merge commit with two parents.
`git branch -d` removes only the label. The commits stay, reached through the merge.

formula.name: Merge a finished branch
formula.note: Check with `git log --oneline --graph`, then `git branch -d experiment`.

summary.trap: `git merge main` while on experiment moves experiment, not main. Merge into the branch you are standing on.

quiz.prose: main has not moved since you made the branch carry. carry has 2 new commits. On main you run `git merge carry`.
quiz.question: How many new commits does main's history gain?

widget.label: New commits
widget.accept: 2: a fast-forward adds no merge commit

feedback.correct: A fast-forward adds the 2 commits and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is there anything to join here?

byKey.merge-commit: You added a merge commit. main was directly behind carry, so git just slides main forward.
byKey.one: Merging keeps every commit. Both of carry's commits join main's history.

explain.text: main was directly behind carry, so the merge was a fast-forward. main now points at carry's newest commit. Its history gained exactly 2 commits.

quiz.prose:
You try to tidy up and see:

```sh
$ git branch -d value-signal
error: the branch 'value-signal' is not fully merged.
```
quiz.question: What is git telling you?

options.text: value-signal has commits that the current branch does not contain
The branch is damaged and cannot be deleted
options.why: Nothing is damaged. git is protecting commits only that label reaches.

options.text: Half of a merge is still in progress
options.why: The message is about deleting, not merging. It checks what would be lost.

options.text: Some files in your folder are unsaved
options.why: `-d` looks at commits, not at your folder.

feedback.correct: Deleting the label would leave its commits unreachable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about which commits only that label reaches.

explain.text: Some commits are reachable only from value-signal. Deleting the label would strand them, so `-d` refuses. Merge first, or use `-D` if you really want to throw them away.

quiz.prose: Your new signal is finished on the branch carry. You want it in main.
quiz.question: Which commands do that?

options.text: `git switch main`, then `git merge carry`
`git switch carry`, then `git merge main`
options.why: That brings main into carry. main itself does not move.

options.text: `git merge carry` while on carry
options.why: carry already contains itself. git says Already up to date.

options.text: `git branch -d carry` from main
options.why: Deleting the label does not move its work into main. git would refuse, as carry is not merged.

feedback.correct: Stand on main, then merge carry in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A merge moves the branch you are on.

explain.text: A merge moves only the branch HEAD is on. So you switch to main first, then name carry. main then contains carry's work.

quiz.prose:
Part of a `git log --oneline --graph`:

```sh
*   e81c2d4 Merge branch 'carry'
|\
| * 5b20f1e Add carry signal
* | 90aa7c3 Fix costs
|/
* 12d9e07 Load prices
```
quiz.question: How many parents does e81c2d4 have?

feedback.correct: A merge commit has two parents: 90aa7c3 and 5b20f1e.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the lanes leaving e81c2d4.

byKey.one: e81c2d4 has two lanes below it. A merge commit joins two lines of work.
byKey.all: Parents are the commits directly below in each lane: 90aa7c3 and 5b20f1e. 12d9e07 is further back.

explain.text: The `|\` under e81c2d4 opens a second lane. Its parents are 90aa7c3 in the left lane and 5b20f1e in the right one. That makes it a merge commit.
